The crack textures (DamageDetail, DamageDetailNormal) do not need overriding: one pair suits brick, concrete, stone and plaster. Swap them only for a different kind of break, such as wood splinters or torn metal. The crack texture is made for mineral materials, so metal and glass look best with their own detail textures.

docs.title: Keep your own material: the two functions
docs.text:
If you already have a good material, for example with roughness and AO maps, keep it and wire in the two functions instead:

TexCoord[0] (× your tiling)  --> MF_GridDamageUV.UV
MF_GridDamageUV.FaceUV       --> the UVs input of EVERY surface Texture Sample
                                 (colour, normal, roughness, AO)
MF_GridDamageUV.DetailUV     --> MF_GridDamage.DetailUV
your albedo at its smallest mip --> MF_GridDamage.SurfaceAverage   (optional)
  (a Texture Sample of your albedo: MipValueMode = MipLevel, MipValue = 14,
   UVs = Constant2 0.5, 0.5. Unwired, dust is neutral grey)
your broken-material texture --> MF_GridDamage.DamagedColor   (optional,
  with UVs = FaceUV; used when DamagedMapAmount > 0)
your BaseColor / Roughness / Normal --> the inputs of MF_GridDamage
MF_GridDamage: BaseColor / Roughness / Normal --> the material's pins
MF_GridDamage.AO             --> Ambient Occlusion (multiply with your own AO)

The Grid Damage parameters appear in your material's instances, and everything above applies to them.

Without FaceUV on the textures there is no parallax: the surface textures must take their UVs from FaceUV, or the offset has nothing to move.

docs.title: Parallax: where it is and how to see it
docs.text:
The parallax is kept cheap, so it is subtle by nature:

  • It works only where there is depth: in dents and open cracks. On an intact wall the offset is zero.
  • It shows only at an angle. Straight on the offset is close to zero, which is physically right. Walk along the wall and look at a dent from the side.
  • To check it is wired: set ParallaxDepth to 0.1 for a moment and look at a dent at an angle. The texture inside the chips should sink and swim. Then set it back to 0.02–0.03.
  • If nothing changes with your own material, the textures are not taking FaceUV.

Most of the depth still comes from the dent's geometry, the chip normal and the AO; parallax adds the sense of "inward".

docs.title: The data under the material
docs.text: Use this to write your own damage material, or to check the data is arriving. Every vertex of a wall's visual mesh carries four damage channels and a second UV set, filled on every rebuild, at 20 bytes per vertex. The collider never carries them.

docs.title: Vertex colour
docs.text:
channel carries range use it for R remaining material at this vertex: the thickness left, or what side cuts have left of a cell's width, whichever is lower 1 intact → 0 eaten through crack masks, roughness, depth, tint toward the interior colour G breach proximity 1 at an opened cell → 0 at BreachFalloffCells dust, soot, crack density, aggregate around a hole B interior-surface mask 1 on rim and cap quads, 0 on the two faces the material switch: Lerp(FaceFinish, InteriorFinish, B) A which face 1 front, 0 back a different finish per side. Read it only where B is 0: Lerp(Back, Front, A * (1 - B))

B is the one that earns the feature. A hole's rim and a capped edge are the broken thickness a player looks into. Without B a rim inherits the face's brick or plaster, and the hole reads as a cut in paper. Wire B first, then R, then G.

R always matches the geometry the player sees, and every machine computes the same values.

docs.title: UV1
docs.text: TexCoord index 1: 0..1 across the whole wall on both axes, whatever its size, and independent of UV Tile Cm. It does not move when the wall is damaged. Use it for anything that should stay put on the wall: a grime gradient from the floor up, a decal atlas, a per-wall variation mask.

docs.title: Seeing a channel with your own eyes
docs.text:
Make a scratch material with Shading Model: Unlit and plug VertexColor into Emissive Color. Put it in the preset's WallMaterial (not on the actor) and press Apply Preset. Shoot the wall: red fades toward black in craters (R), green blooms around openings (G), and every rim and capped edge is blue (B). For UV1, plug TexCoord index 1 into Emissive: a clean red-green gradient across the wall, unchanged by shooting it.

  • B flat: the wall has no rim to show. Check HoleRimThicknessFraction and CapEdges.
  • G flat: BreachFalloffCells is 0, or nothing has gone through yet.
  • Everything flat: bEmitDamageAttributes is off on the placed actor.

docs.title: What you see → what to turn
docs.text:
symptom cause and fix a light or white patch around damage that is dust. It takes the texture's average colour, so a light patch means DustTint is too high or, with your own material, SurfaceAverage is not wired. Set DustAmount to 0 to check the whole wall is white or light grey BaseColorMap is not set: the default is a white texture the whole wall is darker than before BaseTint is not white a checkerboard or an error on NormalMap the normal texture's Compression is not Normalmap nothing changes on hits the material did not reach the wall (run CheckPresets), bEmitDamageAttributes is off, or DentGain is too low one bullet chips the whole dent lower DentGain cracks are huge or tiny DetailTiling a repeating pattern shows give DetailTiling a fractional part the texture swims as the camera moves lower ParallaxDepth no parallax see Parallax a hole's rims look like the face channel B: check HoleRimThicknessFraction chips on the back opposite a dent expected: R is the total thickness, so the back also "sees" the dent. It reads as spalling from behind the chip edge follows the cell grid the mask is interpolated between vertices. Finer cells (SubdivisionFactor) or a higher DetailTiling help the patch edge is blurry AreaSoftness is too high the patch edge shimmers far away raise AreaSoftness to 2

If your symptom is not here, send a close and a distant screenshot of the wall with the instance's Details panel.

docs.title: Effects and sounds
docs.text:
Walls fire their own effects and sounds, where material actually came off, on every client. The weapon does not fire them at the bullet's point, a shot that opens nothing spawns nothing, and a player who joins mid-fight does not see old damage replayed.

It works out of the box. The shipped DA_GridSurfaceMaterials has Niagara systems and sounds assigned for every material, and every GridDestructibleWall adds a GridDestructionFXComponent at runtime that plays them. There is nothing to wire. Nothing here replicates, and nothing plays on a dedicated server.

Keep your weapon's impact effect

It is instant for the shooter. The wall's effects arrive with replication, one network update later on a client. The weapon says "hit"; the wall says "this is what broke".

docs.title: The slots
docs.text:
Each row of the surface material asset (Configs → a material → Effects) has four effect slots and three sound slots.

slot fires once per +X points User parameters BreakFX material opens: a hole, an exit blowout, a cut through an end or a bore cluster of fine cells that opened together out of the face the material broke out through: the back for a shot from the front, the side itself for a cut through a cap or jamb CellCount, ExtentCm, Normal, ParticleBudget, ExitsBack, ExitsSide CollapseFX a piece of wall breaks away falling piece out of the wall's front SizeCm, CellCount, Normal LandingFX a falling piece hits something hard piece, once up SizeCm, CellCount, ImpactSpeed ImpactDustFX a hit knocks material off a face or a side without opening anything patch; at most MaxDustPerBatch per batch out of the face that lost it CellCount, RemovedDepthCm, ExtentCm, Normal sound slot plays notes BreakSound with BreakFX a short crunch with variations CollapseSound with CollapseFX; when set, BreakSound does not also play for those cells a heavy crack LandingSound with LandingFX the rubble must simulate physics
  • Fine resolution. Breaks and dust are detected per fine cell, so a bullet hole smaller than a cell fires them.
  • Drawn once. Cells opened by a collapse fire BreakFX only if CollapseFX is empty. A hole fires BreakFX, not dust as well. A corner shared by two joined walls fires on one wall only.
  • Niagara or Cascade. A slot accepts either.

docs.title: Parameters a system receives
docs.text:
The system spawns rotated: local +X points as in the table above, and +Z up the wall (if +X itself points up or down, +Z points out of the wall's face). Author everything that should fly "out" along local +X, and everything that lies along the wall in local Y/Z. The effect then turns to fit any wall, including a sloped one.

Declare the parameters in the system's User Parameters, with exactly these names and types. A parameter the wall does not set keeps its default, and a typo means the parameter always stays at its default.

parameter type meaning User.ExtentCm float half the size of the break or patch: about 5–15 cm for a bullet, 50–150 cm for a grenade. The main scale parameter User.ParticleBudget int already scaled by sg.EffectsQuality (Low 3 / Medium 8 / High 15) and never above CellCount. Use it as the number of chunks User.CellCount int how many fine cells opened: 1–4 for a bullet at subdivision 3, tens to hundreds for a grenade User.Normal vector the wall's outward direction User.ExitsBack, User.ExitsSide bool the break came out of the back, or out of a side User.SizeCm float size of a falling piece User.ImpactSpeed float landing speed, usually 250–1500 cm/s User.RemovedDepthCm float how much material a dent removed in total: 1–5 cm for one bullet

docs.title: Tuning on the wall
docs.text:
knob on default what it does MaxSpawnDistanceCm GridDestructionFX 6000 skips effects far from the local camera MinSoundIntervalSeconds GridDestructionFX 0.08 shortest gap between two sounds of one kind from one wall, so automatic fire does not become a wall of noise SoundVolumeScale GridDestructionFX 1 the wall's overall volume bEmitDust GridDebrisSpawner on turns the dent dust off MaxDustPerBatch GridDebrisSpawner 4 caps dust per batch DustMinErosionBytes GridDebrisSpawner 3 ignores the trickle the far-face coupling adds around a hit LandingMinSpeedCmS GridCollapseVisual 250 how fast a piece must be moving for a sudden stop to count as a landing

Per-wall override. In a wall Blueprint, add GridDestructionFXComponent yourself, tick bOverrideMaterialEffects and fill OverrideEffects. The wall does not add a second one.

The shipped sounds share SCon_GridDestruction (a Sound Concurrency) and SA_GridDestruction (attenuation) in /GridDestruction/Audio/. A grenade opens many clusters at once, so keep a concurrency limit on any sounds you assign.

docs.title: Making your own systems
docs.text: The shipped systems are a starting point. When you replace them, these are the rules that make wall effects read as physical.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text:
Real destruction is three things at once, and a fake-looking effect almost always shows only one:

layer what it is how it behaves chunks pieces of 1–8 cm leave fast, fall on a parabola, bounce once and lie still grit sand, under 1 cm fastest, short-lived, barely visible one by one dust a cloud starts fast, brakes hard, grows 2–4×, settles and fades over 2–4 s
  • Dust is the wall's colour, lighter and greyer. Brick dusts reddish, concrete grey; wood gives splinters and sawdust rather than dust.
  • Timing. Chunks and grit are done in the first 0.1 s; dust lives 20–40 times longer.
  • Size follows the hole. Scale by ExtentCm. A bullet hole with a cloud the size of half the wall reads worse than no effect.
  • Lit particles. Unlit dust glows in shadow. Use a lit translucent material (Volumetric PerVertex NonDirectional is cheap) with Depth Fade 20–50 cm.

docs.title: Chunks (GPU)
docs.text:
1. Sim target GPU, local space off, fixed bounds on (about ±300 cm).
  2. Spawn burst: count = User.ParticleBudget.
  3. Spawn position: a box (2, ExtentCm × 2, ExtentCm × 2) in local space, not a point: the YZ plane is the wall.
  4. Velocity: a cone around local +X, 35–55°, 150–600 cm/s. Smaller pieces faster. Optionally 20–30% at half speed along −X: the entry side loses grit too.
  5. Gravity and drag 0.4–1.2: without drag every piece flies the same arc.
  6. Mesh renderer with 4–6 chunk meshes, random index and rotation, sizes weighted to the small end.
  7. GPU depth-buffer collision, restitution 0.05–0.2, high friction.
  8. Freeze on first contact. When the collision flag is set, zero the velocity, gravity and drag, and the rotation rate (or scale it by saturate(length(Velocity) / 50)), or a landed chip spins until its lifetime ends. A settled particle then costs rendering only, and depth-buffer collision, which only knows what is on screen, no longer matters to it.
  9. Scale the mesh to 0 over the last 10% of its life.

docs.title: Dust
docs.text: CPU is fine (few particles). 4–12 sprites from a disc of radius ExtentCm × 0.6 in the YZ plane; velocity along +X 100–300 cm/s in a 30–45° cone with drag 3–6, so the cloud bursts out and hangs; size grows ×2–4 over its life; alpha peaks at 0.25–0.5 quickly and fades slowly; life 1.5–4 s; slow rotation and a weak curl noise.

docs.title: Per material
docs.text: Concrete Brick Stone Wood Metal Glass chunks angular rubble brick fragments and grey mortar larger angular rubble splinters, 3–12 cm torn strips, few flat shards, many cone half-angle 45° 40° 35° 55° 30° 70° speed, cm/s 200 200 150 260 120 350 drag 0.6 0.6 0.5 1.2 0.4 0.9 restitution 0.05 0.05 0.05 0.10 0.15 0.20 dust colour (linear) 0.45 0.44 0.42 0.50 0.34 0.26 0.42 0.40 0.37 0.55 0.45 0.32, little none none special — two chunk colours — sawdust instead of dust sparks: short, bright, velocity-aligned high specular, roughness 0.05

docs.title: Recipes per slot
docs.text:
• BreakFX = chunks + grit + dust. Multiply count and speed by ExitsBack ? 1.3 : 1.0 for a bigger exit than entry. For a bullet keep it short and modest (3–8 chunks, 4–6 puffs, gone in 2 s); a grenade is the same system scaled by its parameters. Check both.
  • ImpactDustFX is the most frequent effect, so keep it the cheapest: 3–6 puffs, alpha ≤ 0.3, life 1–2 s, scaled by clamp(RemovedDepthCm / 4, 0.4, 1.5).
  • CollapseFX: large, slow dust from the piece's volume (30–120 cm/s, grows ×3, 3–5 s, settles down) and 10–30 small pieces falling from the break with almost no initial speed.
  • LandingFX: +X is up, so the YZ plane is the floor. A ring of dust of radius SizeCm × 0.5, moving radially outward at 80–250 cm/s with drag 3–5, strength clamp((ImpactSpeed − 250) / 1000, 0.3, 1).

docs.title: Performance rules
docs.text:
The component takes systems from Niagara's pool and culls them by distance. For that to work:

  1. Every system must finish. All emitters Loop Behavior Once, the system's Inactive Response Complete or Kill. An endless emitter never returns to the pool: a leak you only see after an hour of play.
  2. Give the systems an Effect Type with a max distance around 6000 cm, an instance cap of 16–32 per system, and scalability by sg.EffectsQuality. Its visibility culling must Deactivate, not Pause: a paused system off screen keeps its particles forever.
  3. GPU emitters need fixed bounds.
  4. No per-pixel sorting, distortion or lights on dust. Light renderers only for metal sparks, only on High.
  5. Check: stat Niagara after a minute of shooting should level off, not climb. fx.DumpNCPoolInfo shows pooled components in use.

docs.title: Checklist per material
docs.text:
• dust matches the wall's colour, but lighter
  • dust brakes and grows rather than flying evenly
  • chunks vary in size, small ones fly further
  • one system gives a small bullet effect and a large grenade effect
  • a shot through from the front throws chunks out of the back
  • a shot into an end or a reveal dusts out of that side
  • particles are lit (check in shadow)
  • the system finishes (pool instances do not grow)
  • it looks decent on Low

docs.title: Driving your own effects from events
docs.text:
To spawn effects yourself instead of through the slots, leave the slots empty and bind the wall's events. GridDebrisSpawnerComponent spawns nothing itself: it watches cells open, groups them into clusters, applies a budget, primes a baseline so a joining client does not replay every old hole, and broadcasts.

event on fires OnDebrisBurstBP GridDebrisSpawner once per cluster of opened cells, with FGridDebrisBurst OnDustBP GridDebrisSpawner a dent that opened nothing OnChunkDetachedBP GridCollapseVisual a piece breaks away OnChunkLandedBP GridCollapseVisual a falling piece lands

The collapse events fire after the component has finished its own work, so a listener may damage the wall safely.

FGridDebrisBurst:

field use it for WorldLocation where to spawn: the cluster centre, on the wall's mid-surface WorldNormal the wall's outward direction, always the front ExitNormal, bExitsBack, bExitsSide which way to throw: out of the face the material broke out through CellCount how many cells opened, counted at the finest level. Scale the burst; never spawn per cell ExtentCm half-size of the cluster: how wide to spread the spawn Surface which system and material to pick bFromCollapse the cells were opened by a collapse SuggestedParticleCount already scaled by sg.EffectsQuality

One system per surface type beats one system with a switch: the mesh, material and size distribution all differ.

docs.title: What this deliberately does not do
docs.text:
• Particles are never shootable and never block anything. Settled geometry that blocked shots would stand in a different place on every machine, because rubble does not replicate. Nothing in gameplay depends on where particles land.
  • A doorway-sized plank is not a particle. Particles work at fist scale and below. A large falling piece is real geometry for about a second, from GridCollapseVisualComponent; particles carry what is left on the floor.
  • Two clients may disagree about the dust. That is fine, and it costs no bandwidth.

docs.title: Blueprint API: wiring your weapons
docs.text: What to call, from where, and what the plugin never asks of you.

docs.title: The one thing to know
docs.text:
The plugin never looks for your weapons. Your weapon calls the plugin.

There is no damage pipeline to opt into, no interface your projectile has to implement, no component your character needs, and no dependency on the Gameplay Ability System. Wherever your game already decides "this shot hit that surface", you add one function call.

docs.title: Two entry points. Pick one.
docs.text:
Path A: direct Path B: tag table Call Apply Grid Damage on GridDataComponent Notify Hit By Tag on GridDestructionBridgeComponent You supply every number: depth, radius, face where the hit landed and which way it was going Numbers come from your call site a data asset, keyed by GameplayTag Needs nothing one data asset Needs GameplayTags no yes Good for one weapon, a prototype, a system that already has per-weapon numbers a shipping game with a weapon table

Both are BlueprintCallable, both are server-only, and both do the same thing once the numbers are resolved: Path B is Path A with a lookup in front of it. Start on A; move to B when you have more than a couple of weapons.

docs.title: Path A: no Bridge, no tags, no GAS
docs.text:
Everything you need is on the GridDataComponent that every wall already has. After your trace, in Blueprint or C++:

  1. From the hit actor, Get Component by Class → GridDataComponent. None means it is not a destructible wall; that is your branch.

  2. Fill an FGridDamageParams:

    field value HitLocation the impact point, world space HitDirection the direction the round was travelling, normalised PeakDepthCm how deep it bites into reference material; a rifle bullet is 3–5 RadiusCm the crater's radius. 0 lets the wall's preset decide (MinSpallRadiusCells, a crater of a cell or more). 2–5 cm leaves a small mark for a pistol round, on walls that subdivide. Above that, a blast ImpactFace leave at Auto: it is derived from HitDirection

  3. Call Apply Grid Damage.

That is the whole integration, and it works from a Blueprint-only project.

Use the shot's travel direction, not the surface normal

The crater is shaped by the angle the round arrived at, so a glancing hit leaves a furrow along its path. The impact normal is the surface's normal and throws exactly that away. In a trace, the direction is Normalize(TraceEnd − TraceStart).

Apply Grid Damage returns an FGridDamageResult: which cells opened, whether the wall was penetrated, how much penetration depth is left for whatever is behind it, Obliquity and bGrazing. Read it if you want the round to carry on through, or to spark off a ricochet.

docs.title: Path B: the tag table
docs.text:
Worth the setup as soon as "how deep does a 7.62 go into brick" stops being a number you want at a call site.

Every GridDestructibleWall adds a GridDestructionBridgeComponent to itself at BeginPlay. To opt a wall out, clear that entry from its CompanionComponents list. For an actor with a GridDataComponent that is not a GridDestructibleWall, call Get Or Add Grid Bridge: it returns the one there, or adds one.

Create the weapon table, in this order:

  1. One or more GridImpactProfile data assets, each holding the numbers: PeakDepthCm, RadiusCm, bIsPenetrating.
  2. One GridImpactProfileSet. Each row is a GameplayTag and a profile asset. Set DefaultProfile so an unmapped weapon does something visible instead of nothing. The picker lists only saved profiles, so it is empty until step 1 is done.

At the call site: Notify Hit By Tag, passing the set, the weapon's tag, the impact point and the direction.

Resolution is hierarchical. A hit tagged Damage.Type.Rifle.556 uses a row for Damage.Type.Rifle.556 if there is one, otherwise Damage.Type.Rifle, then Damage.Type. Ship one row for a whole family and override a single calibre when it earns it.

It returns false when no row matched and there is no default, so "this weapon is not in the table" is distinguishable from "the wall ignored it".

docs.title: GAS
docs.text:
There is nothing GAS-specific to do. Call Notify Hit By Tag from wherever your damage lands: a Gameplay Ability, a GameplayEffectExecutionCalculation reading the hit from the effect's context, or a target-data callback. The tag you pass is usually one the Gameplay Effect already carries.

Walls have no Ability System Component and do not need one. If your damage pipeline only applies effects to actors with an ASC, it skips walls silently. Call the plugin where you have the hit result, before the ASC check.

docs.title: Any weapon system
docs.text:
The plugin does not care what fired.

weapon call Hitscan once per hit; RadiusCm = 0 for the preset's crater, or a few cm for a small round Projectile from your impact handler, with the projectile's velocity as the direction Explosion one call at the blast centre with RadiusCm set. You do not find the cells yourself Melee, thrown, vehicle impact the same call Lyra Starter Game step by step in Example: Lyra Starter Game

docs.title: Authority
docs.text:
Every entry point is server-only and does nothing on a client. Cell state replicates from the server; clients render what they are told. That makes the calls safe in code that runs on both machines, such as a weapon ability or a shared damage function, without guarding them yourself.

Called only on a client, nothing happens and nothing is logged

"I call it and the wall does not break" is almost always this. Check Has Authority on the calling actor first.

For multiplayer, add GridNetClientComponent to your PlayerController or pawn. It needs no code: it lets a client ask the server to resend a wall that went out of sync, so it heals at once. See Multiplayer.

docs.title: Other calls worth knowing
docs.text: call on what it does Capture Damage Snapshot / Apply Damage Snapshot GridDataComponent save and restore a wall's damage (Setup) Reset Damage the wall back to its Initial Damage, else intact (server)

docs.title: Example: Lyra Starter Game
docs.text: The plugin was also tested in a copy of Epic's Lyra Starter Game, a common starting point for shooters. Lyra needs no adapter and no code: the wiring below is a few Blueprint nodes and two data assets in your project, and nothing in Lyra's source changes. It is also a worked example of Path B for any GAS-based weapon system.

docs.title: 1. Walls
docs.text: Place GridDestructibleWalls and apply presets as usual. Lyra's weapons trace on Lyra_TraceChannel_Weapon, and Lyra's DefaultEngine.ini makes the BlockAll profile block it; the wall's collider uses BlockAll. If you give the collider your own profile, make it block that channel.

docs.title: 2. Impact numbers
docs.text:
Lyra never calls TakeDamage, so a weapon hit is passed to the wall through the tag table (Path B):

  1. A GridImpactProfile data asset, for example DA_Impact_Bullet: Peak Depth Cm 3–5, Radius Cm 0.
  2. A GridImpactProfileSet, for example DA_GridImpacts_Lyra: Default Profile = DA_Impact_Bullet. Add rows (Tag → Profile) per weapon later.

docs.title: 3. Hitscan weapons
docs.text:
Content Browser → Settings → Show Plugin Content, then open GA_Weapon_Fire from ShooterCore (the parent of GA_Weapon_Fire_Pistol and the others; if the children's parent is the C++ class LyraGameplayAbility_RangedWeapon, edit each child instead). In its Event Graph, find Event On Ranged Weapon Target Data Ready:

  1. Put a Sequence after the event: Then 0 → Lyra's existing damage logic (Ctrl-drag the existing wire, do not delete it); Then 1 → the nodes below.
  2. For Loop from 0 to Get Data Count From Target Data (Target Data) − 1.
  3. In the loop body: Get Hit Result From Target Data (Target Data, Index) → Break Hit Result.
  4. Hit Actor → Get Or Add Grid Bridge → Is Valid (not a wall: skip).
  5. On the Bridge: Notify Hit By Tag with
    • Profile Set = DA_GridImpacts_Lyra, Impact Tag empty (the set's Default Profile) or the weapon's tag;
    • Origin = Impact Point;
    • Hit Direction = Normalize(Trace End − Trace Start);
    • Hit Instigator = Get Avatar Actor From Actor Info.
  6. Compile and save. Children without their own On Ranged Weapon Target Data Ready inherit this; a child that has one overrides it, so add the same nodes there or Add Call to Parent Function.

The event also runs on the client (shot prediction). That is fine: Notify Hit By Tag does nothing off the server and returns false there.

Worked when

A shot in a listen-server PIE session makes a hole in both windows, and Notify Hit By Tag returns true on the server. False on the server: the set has no profile for the tag and no Default Profile. No hole and the node never runs: the shot went through a child ability with its own event (step 6).

docs.title: 4. Grenades and projectiles
docs.text: In the explosion's or projectile's impact Blueprint, on the server: the same Get Or Add Grid Bridge → Notify Hit By Tag, at the blast centre, with a profile whose Radius Cm is set. One call per blast; the wall finds the cells.

docs.title: 5. Fast resync
docs.text: Put GridNetClientComponent on the controller: open the ShooterCore GameFeatureData (or your Experience's) → Actions → Add Components → Actor Class LyraPlayerController, Component Class GridNetClientComponent, Client ✓ Server ✓. Lyra sets MaxClientRate to 200000, so the default MaxBytesPerSecond leaves room for everything else.

docs.title: Cost at the call site
docs.text:
• Path A is a component lookup and a function call. No allocation.
  • Path B adds a walk over your profile rows once per hit. Tag comparison is name comparison, not string comparison.
  • Neither path allocates per shot. The damage work is proportional to the cells the hit touches, not to the size of the wall.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text: Damage is decided on the server, and every client renders the same cells. This page covers testing it, the bandwidth budgets and keeping clients in sync.

docs.title: Testing in the editor
docs.text:
Play dropdown → Number of Players = 2, Net Mode = Play As Listen Server. Damage a wall from the server window; the hole appears on the client within about one network update.

Once per session, or after changing anything about replication, type in either window while PIE is running:

GridDestruction.HashCells

It hashes every live world and prints its own verdict:

GRIDHASH [Server/PIE] WORLD: hash=0x4B10D8F2 over 3 wall(s).
GRIDHASH [Client/PIE] WORLD: hash=0x4B10D8F2 over 3 wall(s).
GRIDHASH VERDICT: MATCH across 2 worlds.

MATCH means both machines hold the same cell data, so anything that still looks wrong is in the mesh, not the network. MISMATCH prints the first cell where they disagree, and how.

Run it during play: after PIE ends only the editor world is left, and the command refuses to give a verdict over one world. Each wall's line also carries net=… epoch=… match, the server's published hash for that wall against this machine's own, so one window's log already says whether it agrees. Between two PCs, compare the world hash on each machine's net panel (below).

docs.title: What replicates
docs.text:
Only damaged cells. An undamaged wall costs nothing after its first update, and a late joiner receives only the cells that were actually hit.

Rubble, effects, sounds and the damage material's look do not replicate: every machine derives them from the cells.

docs.title: Bandwidth and budgets
docs.text:
Project Settings → Plugins → Grid Destruction — Network holds every budget:

setting default what it trades ItemsPerShardPerFlush 128 Cells one wall sends per update. Lower: holes appear over a few more frames under heavy fire, with flatter peaks. Keep it well under 512: the engine refuses an update over 2048 changes, and a lost packet merges updates. MinFlushIntervalSeconds 0.1 Shortest time between two updates of one wall. MaxBytesPerSecond 65536 All walls together. Keep it well under your project's MaxClientRate (engine default 100000, Lyra 200000): damage shares the connection with movement. BurstBytes 32768 How much may go out at once after a quiet spell, such as the first grenade. bKeyframeAfterQuiet on After a wall has been quiet, resend the cells the last burst changed, once, from what new damage leaves of the budget. Heals a client that missed an update. KeyframeQuietSeconds 3 How long "quiet" is. DesyncCheckDelaySeconds 0.5 How long a client waits for data to settle before it compares its wall with the server's. ResyncRequestCooldownSeconds 2 Shortest time between two resends of one wall on request, and between two requests from one player. LateJoinWarnBytes 49152 Walls whose worst case is over this get a warning at start (below).

If holes lag under very heavy fire (cutters, grenade spam), the byte budget is what limits it. A brick cell at subdivision 4 costs up to about 62 bytes, so the default budget carries roughly 1000 cells per second across all walls. Raise MaxBytesPerSecond if your MaxClientRate has room, or lower SubdivisionFactor.

GridNet.Measure (on the server, development builds) prints what each wall costs on the network now, in bytes, and its worst case.

docs.title: Desync detection and self-heal
docs.text: The server publishes a hash per wall. A client compares each wall with it; when they still differ on a second look, it logs a DESYNC warning and asks the server to resend the wall, and the resent cells overwrite the wrong ones. GridDestruction.HashCells shows the result.

docs.title: Fast resync
docs.text: Add GridNetClientComponent to your PlayerController, or to the pawn, so a client can ask for that resend at once. Without it the wall still heals, at the server's next resend after KeyframeQuietSeconds. The component needs no code. In a GameFeature-based project such as Lyra, add it to the PlayerController class with an Add Components action.

docs.title: The net panel
docs.text:
With bShowNetDebug on the component (the sample character has it on; H or GridNet.ToggleDebug toggles it), each machine draws a panel: role, ping, connection rates, how many walls match the server's published hash, the world hash (HashCells' number: equal on two PCs means equal walls), items sent or received, DESYNCs, and the busiest walls. A wall reads settling while its data is still arriving, and MISMATCH only once the detector confirms it. Every 5 seconds it also logs a GRIDNET STAT line, so two machines' logs can be compared afterwards. The panel is compiled out of Shipping builds.

To watch the heal: GridNet.CorruptCell <Wall> <Cell> (development builds) changes one damaged cell on this machine only.

docs.title: Late-join size
docs.text:
A joining client receives each wall's damaged cells in one update, and the engine refuses one over about 64 KB. A wall that could exceed LateJoinWarnBytes when fully damaged logs a warning at start, and GridDestruction.CheckPresets lists it in the editor. A 48×48 wall is about 32 KB at subdivision 1 and about 140 KB at subdivision 4. Three ways out:

  1. lower SubdivisionFactor or the grid size;
  2. split the wall into two walls (joined walls behave as one);

  3. raise the limit on both server and client, in DefaultEngine.ini:

    [ConsoleVariables]
net.MaxConstructedPartialBunchSizeBytes=262144

A rejoining player gets every wall back with its damage, not instantly: the damaged cells arrive at the connection's rate, then the meshes rebuild.

docs.title: Replication system and cheating
docs.text:
Replication system. Built and tested on the default (legacy) replication system. Iris is untested; the server logs a warning if it runs with Iris.

Dedicated servers. Walls simulate damage and structure there, and spawn no effects or sounds. A dedicated server cannot read textures, so a wall's break pattern (the fracture mask or its material's height map) is baked when you save the level, and the server uses that. Save the level after changing a wall's material, mask or size. A wall spawned at runtime on a dedicated server has no saved pattern: it breaks by the default pattern, with a warning in the log.

Cheating. Damage is decided on the server, and shots and movement are checked against the server's collider. Detecting memory edits or wallhacks belongs to your game's anti-cheat (EAC, BattlEye), not to this plugin.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: From an empty project to a wall that breaks, in about ten minutes. Each step says what you should see when it worked, because most failures in a destruction setup are silent and look like "nothing happened".

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
From Fab. In the Epic Games Launcher, open Library → Fab Library, find Grid Destruction and click Install to Engine for your engine, 5.7 or 5.8. Then, in your project, open Edit → Plugins, search for Grid Destruction, tick it and restart the editor.

Into one project. Create a Plugins/ folder in the project root, and put the plugin at Plugins/GridDestruction/, so that this folder directly contains GridDestruction.uplugin. For a C++ project, right-click the .uproject → Generate Visual Studio project files, open the .sln, pick Development Editor and build.

Worked when

The editor opens and GridDestructibleWall appears in the Place Actors panel.

docs.title: 2. Play the showcase
docs.text:
The plugin ships a showcase level, so you can see every material break before you set anything up.

  1. In the Content Browser, open Settings → Show Plugin Content.
  2. Open Plugins → GridDestruction Content → Demo → L_GridDestruction_Showcase and press Play.

  3. You play a third-person UE Mannequin with four weapons:

    key action WASD move Space jump left mouse button fire; hold for the cutter; throw the grenade 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 rifle / breaching charge / cutter / grenade mouse wheel cycle weapons R reset every wall H show or hide the network panel

The level has every shipped material, built-up walls, doors and windows with glass, piers carrying a beam, a room with a roof, a cantilever, stacked walls and a corner of two materials, each one labelled. Every wall in it is an ordinary GridDestructibleWall with a GP_* preset, so select one to see how it is set up.

docs.title: 3. Your first wall
docs.text:
1. Drag GridDestructibleWall into your level.
  2. In its Details panel, set Preset to one of the shipped presets, for example GP_Brick (in /GridDestruction/Presets/).
  3. Click Apply Preset.

Worked when

The Output Log shows two lines like these, with your wall's own numbers:

ApplyPresetToGridData [GridDestructibleWall_0]: preset='GP_Brick' grid 16x12, cell 25.0cm, ...
Grid initialized: 16x12 cells, 25cm each. ... HasAuthority=1, cells=192

Apply Preset is not optional

A preset is stamped onto the wall. A value edited on the preset reaches a placed wall only when you press Apply Preset on that wall, and a value typed on the wall's own component is overwritten the next time you press it. This is the most common reason a setting "does nothing". GridDestruction.CheckPresets lists every wall that is out of date.

docs.title: 4. Break it without a weapon
docs.text:
Press Play, select the wall in the World Outliner, and use the buttons in its Details panel:

button what it is for DealTestDamage(Location, PeakDepthCm, RadiusCm, Face) one hit, precisely placed DealTestDamageRandom(PeakDepthCm) a hit somewhere, to prove the pipe works DealTestBlast(Location, Depth, Radius, Lobes, Raggedness, Seed, Face) a ragged crater instead of a circle

RadiusCm = 0 is a bullet; above 0 is a blast. Pass a non-zero Seed to DealTestBlast and the same crater comes back every time.

Worked when

A dent appears, then a hole, and debris falls from it.

docs.title: 5. Check it in multiplayer
docs.text:
In the Play dropdown set Number of Players = 2 and Net Mode = Play As Listen Server. Damage the wall from the server window: the hole appears on the client too. Then type in either window's console:

GridDestruction.HashCells

GRIDHASH [Server/PIE] WORLD: hash=0x4B10D8F2 over 3 wall(s).
GRIDHASH [Client/PIE] WORLD: hash=0x4B10D8F2 over 3 wall(s).
GRIDHASH VERDICT: MATCH across 2 worlds.

MATCH means both machines hold the same cell data.

docs.title: 6. Connect your weapons
docs.text: One call where your game already knows "this shot hit that surface": Apply Grid Damage on the wall's GridDataComponent. It works from Blueprint, needs no GameplayTags and no GAS, and must run on the server. The Blueprint API page has the details and the tag-table alternative; it also has step-by-step wiring for Lyra Starter Game.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Setup: openings, building tools, floors and ceilings, layered walls, saved damage.
  • Surface presets: every number per material, and the order to tune them in.
  • Damage material: make the shipped material use your textures.
  • Effects and sounds: what the wall fires and how to replace it.
  • Troubleshooting: console commands and the symptoms people actually run into.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: The full path from an installed plugin to walls that look and break right. If you have not yet seen a wall break, start with the Quick start.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
A wall takes almost everything from a GridWallPreset data asset. Seven ship in /GridDestruction/Presets/: GP_Concrete, GP_Concrete_Thin, GP_Brick, GP_Stone, GP_Wood, GP_Metal and GP_Glass.

To make your own: Add → Miscellaneous → Data Asset → GridWallPreset, or duplicate a shipped one. Four fields matter to get something on screen:

field what it does WallMesh the source mesh. Its bounds decide the wall's size, unless the wall overrides it. SurfaceType which material column of Surface presets this wall is ThicknessCm how deep the wall is. Everything about penetration scales off this. CellDensity cells per metre. 4.0 means 25 cm cells.

Everything else has a working default. The numbers per material, and what each one changes, are in Surface presets.

Apply Preset after every edit

A preset is stamped onto the wall. Press Apply Preset on the wall after changing the preset, and do not type values on the wall's component that the preset also sets: the next press overwrites them. A feature set only on the component is simply off. GridDestruction.CheckPresets prints STALE for every wall that is out of date.

docs.title: Placing walls
docs.text:
1. Drag GridDestructibleWall into the level.
  2. Assign the preset to its Preset field.
  3. Click Apply Preset.

docs.title: Sizing a wall
docs.text:
By default the preset's WallMesh decides width and height. To size one wall on its own, tick Wall | Size → Override Wall Size and type Wall Size Cm (width, height). The wall is always a whole number of cells, rounded down, and Resolved Wall Size Cm shows what was built. Editing these re-applies the preset at once.

Keep the actor's scale at 1: scale stretches the cells.

Cell density is a target. The cell actually used is the closest size that divides the wall's width and height exactly (shown as Resolved Cell Size Cm), so changing the density never moves or resizes the wall. Round wall sizes, in multiples of 10 cm, give it plenty to choose from.

docs.title: Pivot and quick building
docs.text:
Wall | Placement → Pivot: Bottom Left puts the pivot on the wall's bottom-left corner as seen from the front, so End drops it on the floor and grid snapping lines walls up edge to edge.

Wall | Build adds a flush copy to the right, to the left, above, or as an outside corner. Press again to keep going from the wall just added. Override Cap Edges closes this wall's own ends: a free-standing end or an outside corner.

docs.title: Viewport handles
docs.text:
Select a wall in the level and handles appear in front of it:

  • Green arrows add a wall to the right, to the left or above.
  • Cyan arrows add an outside corner. The new wall is selected, so you can keep clicking.
  • Yellow points on the right and top edges resize: click one, then drag the move widget (W). The size changes in whole cells and the opposite edge stays put.

Every click and drag is one Ctrl+Z. The handles exist only in the editor.

docs.title: Wall pieces and kits
docs.text:
Make your own pieces once, then build from them.

The plugin ships samples to start from in GridDestruction Content → Variants: concrete and brick walls 400 and 200 cm wide, wood 300 cm, stone 400 cm and glass 200 cm, all 300 cm high, some with a centred door (100 × 200 cm) or window (100 × 100 cm). Four kits group them: WK_Concrete, WK_Brick, WK_Wood and WK_Mixed (every sample). Set one as a wall's Build Kit, or right-click a build arrow with no kit set to pick from every piece in the project. Duplicate a sample into your own folder before you change it: plugin content is replaced when you update the plugin.

  1. Content Browser → right-click → Miscellaneous → Data Asset → Grid Wall Variant. Set a preset, Wall Size Cm, and any doors and windows under Openings. Name it for what it is, for example WV_Brick_400_Window.
  2. Optional: Data Asset → Grid Wall Kit, and list the variants you want together, in menu order: a kit per style or per level.
  3. Place: drag a variant from the Content Browser into the level. It stands on the floor where it is dropped.
  4. Build on: select a wall. A left click on a green or cyan arrow adds that wall's Build Variant, or a copy when none is set; the line above the wall says which. A right click on an arrow opens a menu: a copy, or any piece from the wall's Build Kit (from the whole project when it has none). The piece you pick becomes the new wall's Build Variant, so left clicks keep adding it.

Placing from a variant stamps its values once, like a preset: editing the variant later does not change walls already placed. Source Variant on a wall shows what it was placed from.

docs.title: Openings: doors and windows
docs.text:
Select the GridData component → Grid | Openings → Openings → +. Offset Cm is measured from the wall's bottom-left corner (X along, Y up), and Size Cm is the width and height. The cells are worked out for you and re-worked whenever the density or the wall size changes. Resolved Size Cm shows what was cut, in whole cells, so use multiples of the cell size for an exact fit.

A shot on the reveal of an opening cuts the reveal, not the face.

docs.title: Placing the texture
docs.text:
Each wall has Wall | UV:

field what it does UV Tile Cm centimetres per texture repeat UV Tile Height Cm 0 = square; lets a square texture fit a wall that is not UV Offset Cm slides the texture along or up the wall, to line courses up with a neighbour or the floor UV Rotation Deg rotates it; 90° turns wood grain upright, and the break pattern turns with it

Four buttons do the common cases: UV Stretch To Wall (one texture, corner to corner), UV Fill Wall Keep Aspect (one square texture covering the wall, centred), UV Snap To Whole Tiles (whole repeats, no half brick at the ends) and UV Reset. The preview follows live while you drag.

docs.title: What the Details panel shows
docs.text: The wall shows the preset, the size and the density overrides. The preset shows mesh, material, surface, thickness, density and caps; its tuning is behind the Advanced arrow. On the GridData component, Grid | From Preset is read-only: those values come from the preset, so change them there and press Apply Preset.

docs.title: Anchors: what holds a wall up
docs.text:
A placed wall is anchored at its bottom edge only: the floor holds it. The walls it touches are found on their own and hold the edges they meet, and an anchor on such an edge is ignored.

Set GridData → Grid | Anchors → Anchor Edges by hand only where an edge is built into geometry the plugin does not see:

the wall is Anchor Edges standing on the floor, sides free or joined to other walls Bottom (the default) set in a doorway of a static-mesh building Bottom, Left, Right a span between two static columns Left, Right a ceiling or floor slab resting on walls nothing to do: the walls under it hold it a slab with nothing under it (a balcony) the edges that are built into something

Anchors live on the placed wall, not on the preset, so Apply Preset never changes them. A piece that hangs in the air is almost always held by an anchor on an edge nothing really holds.

docs.title: Joined walls
docs.text:
Walls find their destructible neighbours on their own at BeginPlay. A link is made only at a real joint: two walls end to end, one stacked on another, an L corner, a T-junction, or a wall standing on a destructible floor. Walls that merely stand near each other, cross, or lie face to face are never linked.

  • A joint holds what touches it, if the other side is held up. Two walls that are both cut off do not hold each other up; both fall.
  • A wall stacked on another stands on that wall, so it falls when the wall below is gone.
  • A shot at the joint damages both walls. A blast that reaches across it bites the neighbour too.
  • A small gap is closed. Walls up to SeamToleranceCm apart (2 cm by default) have their facing edges moved half the gap each, so no line of sky shows along the joint.
  • The texture lines up across an end-to-end joint when the wall width is a whole multiple of UV Tile Cm.
  • A two-sided wall material flickers at joints. Keep wall materials one-sided.

bAutoLinkSeams on the preset (on by default) keeps a wall in or out of every joint. GridDestruction.ShowSeams in PIE draws each linked edge in green and joins the two walls with a yellow line.

docs.title: Floors and ceilings
docs.text:
A floor or ceiling is an ordinary wall laid flat, rotated so that its face looks up or down. Lay it on top of the walls that carry it.

  • Clear its anchor edges. A slab resting on walls ignores its anchors anyway, but a slab resting on nothing logs a SLABANCHOR line at the first hit if it still has them.
  • One slab per room, not a carpet of small panels. A single slab is one structural check, held by the walls under it through its own material. Every joint between panels adds a seam, judged more coarsely. Split a ceiling only where it really is several pieces.
  • Overhang past the supporting walls is limited by the preset's MaxOverhangCm. A ceiling built wider than that still stands as built, and loses only what damage leaves overhanging. BuiltOverhangs on the preset picks a stricter rule; see Surface presets.

docs.title: Built-up walls (layers)
docs.text:
A wall can be several of these walls pressed face to face, each with its own preset: plaster over brick, tiles over concrete. Place them parallel with the faces touching, within SeamToleranceCm. Each layer breaks by its own material, and a shot goes through them one at a time.

Concrete over brick: each layer breaks by its own material.

The far-face blowout skips a face that is pressed against another layer, so the layers' holes line up and the wall reads as one. The outer faces keep it. To switch the blowout off on one placement, clear Wall | Damage → Exit Spall on that wall.

docs.title: Where the wall breaks
docs.text:
The break pattern decides which cells give way first. Three sources; the first one that answers wins:

  1. FractureWeightMask on the preset: an explicit texture. This wall breaks this way, full stop.
  2. The height texture of the wall's own material, read automatically. On by default.
  3. A per-cell hash scaled by FractureNoise: rough, but not patterned.

The middle one is the one you will use. Swapping a brick material for a different bond changes how the wall cracks, with nothing to re-author.

You do not have to change the texture's import settings. The bake decodes BC1 to BC5 directly and walks down to a resident mip if the texture streams. BC7 is the one format it refuses, by name: re-import that one texture as BC1, which loses nothing a height map needs.

You do not have to name the height parameter either. Height is the first guess. When it misses, the bake searches the material's parameters for one whose name reads as a height map (HeightTexture, Displacement, ORDp…) and logs which it took. A material with no parameters at all is searched by the names of the textures it samples (T_Brick_H, T_Wall_Displacement…). Anything named like a normal map is never chosen. Set FractureHeightParameter only to pin a different one.

Worked when

The log shows one of

FractureMask (material height map): 'T_Brick_ORDp' baked, 2048x2048 texels -> 75x75 fine cells, format=DXT1 mip=0 channel=Blue ...
FractureMask (FractureWeightMask): 'T_Mortar_Mask' baked, ...

Read range= in that line. range=128..128 means the texture is flat: the bake discards it, warns, and the wall keeps the hash. The usual cause is a material whose height slot still holds Unreal's placeholder T_DefaultDisplacement.

Without a height map, an ambient-occlusion map works well for masonry, since the joints are dark: put an ORM texture in FractureWeightMask with FractureMaskChannel = Red. A base colour works in a pinch with Luminance, plus bInvertFractureMask when the mortar is lighter than the bricks.

Is the grid fine enough for the pattern? When the mask repeats (brick courses, planks), the bake checks the repeat against the fine cells: two fine cells per repeat are the minimum, one for the joint and one for the brick. If the wall has fewer, a MASKSCALE line names the SubdivisionFactor that fixes it. Raise SubdivisionFactor first: fine cells exist only where the wall was hit, so it costs nothing on an intact wall.

docs.title: Packed textures (Megascans, ORM, ORDp)
docs.text:
You do not need to unpack anything into a black-and-white texture. Many materials, Megascans among them, keep the height in one channel of a packed texture beside occlusion and roughness. The bake reads a single channel of any texture, so you only tell it which one:

  1. Open the wall's material and find the texture sample that feeds the height or displacement (in a Megascans material it is usually named ORDp, Occlusion, Roughness, Displacement).
  2. Note which output pin of that sample is used for height: R, G, B or A.
  3. On the preset, set FractureMaskChannel to that channel. Auto reads red, which is right only for a dedicated height texture.

For ORDp the height is the Blue channel. The bake's log line names the texture and the channel it read, so one line confirms it:

FractureMask (material height map): 'T_Brick_ORDp' baked, ... channel=Blue ...

docs.title: The wall's material
docs.text:
The visible surface is a procedural mesh, and its material is the preset's WallMaterial, or the first slot of WallMesh when that is unset.

The shipped presets already use the damage material instances MI_Grid_Damage_*. For your own surface, make an instance of M_Grid_DamageWall and set its textures; Damage material walks through it.

The plugin also has a debug lattice, UGridVisualComponent: one cube per cell, hidden by default and allocating nothing until you turn it on. It is a diagnostic overlay, not the wall's material.

docs.title: Rubble and physical materials
docs.text: Set PhysicalSurface on the preset to a physical material. Falling pieces take their density from it, so a concrete slab does not land like a crisp packet, and the collider carries it too, so your existing impact decals and surface-type logic answer correctly. Effects and sounds are covered in Effects and sounds.

docs.title: AI navigation
docs.text:
The wall's collider is part of the navmesh. In the editor it is built with the wall's preview, so a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume goes around the wall: press P in the viewport to check.

For bots to path through breaches, set Project Settings → Navigation Mesh → Runtime → Runtime Generation = Dynamic. The wall then re-registers its collider every time a hole opens or closes (never on a dent), and the engine rebuilds the tiles under it in the background. With the default Static navmesh the walls are still obstacles, but a hole is never walkable.

docs.title: Pre-damaged walls and saved damage (beta)
docs.text:
Beta

Capturing and applying damage works, but the capture workflow is still rough. Follow the steps below exactly; expect the workflow to change in a later version.

A wall's damage can be saved as a snapshot and put back later: to build ruined houses in the editor, or to carry a room's state between game sessions.

docs.title: What a snapshot is
docs.text:
A snapshot is the struct FGridDamageSnapshot: the wall's damaged cells, nothing else. No mesh, no collider, no textures are stored; the wall rebuilds all of those from the cells, exactly as it does after a shot.

A snapshot fits only a wall with the same grid size and SubdivisionFactor, and it carries a format version, so a later plugin version can still read it. Undamaged cells and authored openings are not stored: openings come from the wall itself. So a wall with a few holes is a few kilobytes, and an intact wall is an empty snapshot.

There are two places to keep one:

  • An asset, GridDamagePreset. It holds one snapshot and is saved in your project like any data asset. A wall points at it through Initial Damage. This is for pre-damaged buildings.
  • Your save game. The struct is Blueprint-ready, so it goes into your own SaveGame object and is written with Save Game to Slot like any other variable. This is for carrying damage between sessions.

docs.title: How it is applied
docs.text:
The server applies a snapshot by writing the stored cells into the wall through the same path a shot uses. The wall's mesh and collider are rebuilt from them, and clients receive the cells as ordinary replicated damage. So a snapshot is never sent as a file: the network only ever sees damaged cells.

  • On the server it is silent: no debris, no falling pieces, no effects.
  • A client already watching the wall sees the change arrive like damage, with effects. Apply snapshots at the start of play or on a level load, before players look at the wall. Players who join later receive it silently.
  • It replaces the wall's current damage; it does not add to it.
  • Pieces that had collapsed come back as holes; nothing falls again.
  • A snapshot that does not fit the wall's grid is refused, with a DAMAGESNAPSHOT ... refused line naming both grids.

A wall with an Initial Damage asset has it applied when the level starts, and the editor viewport shows that damage while you edit.

docs.title: A pre-damaged wall, in the editor
docs.text:
One wall plus a small asset per damage state replaces a separate "damaged" prop.

  1. Content Browser → Add → Miscellaneous → Data Asset → GridDamagePreset. Name it, for example DP_House_WallNorth.
  2. Select the wall in the level → Wall | Damage → Initial Damage = that asset.
  3. Press Play and shoot the wall into the shape you want.
  4. Open the console (~) and type GridDestruction.CaptureDamage. Every wall with an Initial Damage asset writes its current damage into that asset; the Output Log says DAMAGESNAPSHOT [...]: captured N cell(s) ....
  5. Stop play and save the asset (File → Save All). The capture changed the asset in memory only; it is kept once it is saved. The wall now starts damaged in every game, and the editor viewport shows the damage.

Capture again at any time: the command replaces the asset's contents. One asset can go on several walls of the same grid size, for example a row of identical ruined walls.

docs.title: Carrying damage between sessions
docs.text:
In Blueprint, on the server:

  1. In your SaveGame class, add a variable of type Map<Name, GridDamageSnapshot>.
  2. Saving: for each Grid Destructible Wall, call Grid Data → Capture Damage Snapshot and add the result to the map under the wall's actor name. Then Save Game to Slot.
  3. Loading: after the level is loaded and before players look at it, Load Game from Slot, and for each wall found in the map call Grid Data → Apply Damage Snapshot with its entry. It returns false when the snapshot does not fit the wall.

Actor names are stable for walls placed in the level. Walls you spawn at runtime need a key of your own.

docs.title: Resetting
docs.text: GridDestruction.ResetWalls, or Reset Damage on a wall, returns walls to the damage they started with: their Initial Damage, else intact. The sample character's R key does this.

docs.title: Surface presets
docs.text:
What every preset field does, and the order to tune them in.

The shipped presets already carry these values. GP_Concrete, GP_Brick and the others in /GridDestruction/Presets/ are ready to use, so you do not type anything from this page to get a working wall. The value tables are folded away: open them when you make a preset of your own, want to compare materials, or need to get back to the shipped numbers after experimenting.

Three assets carry them, and the split matters:

asset answers GridSurfaceMaterialDataAsset (shipped: DA_GridSurfaceMaterials) how this material fails: shared by every wall made of it GridWallPreset (shipped: GP_*) what this wall is: thickness, density, how much of it may go GridCollapseVisualComponent on the wall what its rubble does after it falls

Use one project-wide surface material asset and reference it from every preset. A surface type missing from its Configs map falls back to neutral values, so a partial map is valid.

docs.title: Editing the numbers: GridMaterials.csv
docs.text:
Every number in tables 1 and 2 lives in one spreadsheet, Config/GridMaterials.csv in the plugin's folder: one column per preset, one row per field, and a Notes column saying what each does. The plugin's folder is Plugins/GridDestruction/ in your project, or Engine/Plugins/Marketplace/GridDestruction/ for a Fab install. Edit the CSV in Excel, Google Sheets or a text editor, then in the editor choose Tools → Execute Python Script and pick scripts/ue_apply_material_table.py from the same folder. The Python Editor Script Plugin must be enabled (it is by default).

It creates or updates each column's preset (row Asset) and its entry in the surface material asset (DA.* rows), then presses Apply Preset on every wall in the open level that uses one of them. Save the level afterwards. The log prints each field it changed as old -> new.

  • An empty cell leaves that value alone.
  • Point Asset at your own preset to tune it from the table; add a column for a second kind of brick. Two columns of one SurfaceType must agree on the DA.* rows, and the script stops if they do not.
  • WallMesh and WallMaterial take asset paths. A preset the script created has neither, so fill them before a wall uses it.
  • Masks, effects and CapEdges stay on the assets.
  • The CSV wins. A value you changed by hand in the editor is overwritten on the next run unless its cell is empty.
  • It reaches only walls in the open level whose preset is a column. In another level using the same presets, run it there too or press Apply Preset; a wall that missed it logs GRIDSTAMP at BeginPlay.

Work on copies

Copy the shipped GP_* presets and the surface material asset into your project, and point the CSV's Asset and SurfaceMaterialData rows at the copies. A plugin update then never overwrites your tuning.

docs.title: Table 1: the surface material asset
docs.text:
DA_GridSurfaceMaterials → Configs → one row per surface type.

Shipped values: open the table Concrete Brick Stone Wood Metal Glass DamageResistance 1.0 0.9 1.4 0.6 2.0 0.3 FalloffScaleU 1.0 1.6 0.9 3.0 0.8 1.2 FalloffScaleV 1.0 0.7 0.9 1.0 0.8 1.2 SmoothingAngleDeg 30 25 20 35 60 15 RicochetAngleDeg 15 15 18 10 30 0 GrazingDamageScale 0.35 0.35 0.30 0.50 0.10 1.0 EdgeProfile.Style Rounded Square Rounded Shard Rounded Shard EdgeProfile.AmplitudeU 0.30 0.30 0.25 0.30 0.08 0.35 EdgeProfile.AmplitudeV 0.30 0.04 0.25 0.06 0.08 0.35 EdgeProfile.QuantiseU 0 0.15 0 0 0 0 EdgeProfile.QuantiseV 0 0 0 0 0 0 EdgeProfile.DepthNoise 0.25 0.15 0.30 0.20 0.05 0.10 bBrittle false false false false false true BrittleBreakFraction 0.35 0.35 0.35 0.35 0.35 0.35 BrittleShardSizeCm 12 12 12 12 12 12

docs.title: Why each column looks the way it does
docs.text:
• Concrete is the reference: resistance 1.0, chaotic spall on both axes, a circular blast. Every other column is a departure from it.
  • Brick fails along its courses. QuantiseU 0.15 against AmplitudeU 0.30 gives discrete levels that read as mortar joints rather than noise, and AmplitudeV 0.04 keeps the courses straight. FalloffScaleU 1.6 against 0.7 spreads a hit sideways along a course instead of down through one.
  • Stone is the hardest masonry: high resistance, the highest DepthNoise so the crater surface is rough, and a low smoothing angle so chips stay faceted.
  • Wood splits along the grain: FalloffScaleU 3.0 against 1.0 makes a hit reach three times as far along the grain as across it. U and V are the visible texture's axes, so rotating Wall | UV by 90° for upright boards turns the grain with them.
  • Metal deforms rather than breaks: the highest resistance, the smallest edge amplitude and a 60° smoothing angle, so it reads as bent sheet.
  • Glass shatters: the lowest resistance, the largest amplitude and a hard 15° smoothing angle.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text: DamageResistance How much of each bite this material takes. It changes how many shots a wall takes and almost nothing about how it looks. Thickness is the real durability knob; resistance saturates once a blast is deep enough to open a cell. FalloffScaleU / FalloffScaleV The blast's shape along and across the texture. The single most recognisable knob, and it costs nothing. SmoothingAngleDeg Normals are smoothed across folds flatter than this. -1 means unset (the wall mesh component's own value), 0 is flat shading. An angle above atan(halfThickness / cellSize) never engages: at 10 cm cells and 15 cm thickness that limit is 37°. RicochetAngleDeg / GrazingDamageScale What a shallow hit takes off. The angle is measured off the surface: 90 is straight on, 0 is along the wall. Below it the bite ramps down to GrazingDamageScale at 0°. A ricochet angle of 0 means the material never grazes. Keep GrazingDamageScale above 0 for anything that spalls: a skipping round still ploughs a furrow, and a shot that leaves no mark reads as a broken wall. The plugin decides how much material came off; whether the projectile deflects, sparks or stops is your weapon's call, using Obliquity and bGrazing in the damage result. EdgeProfile.Style How a hole's outline is drawn. Square follows the cells' sides, honest for brick. Shard cuts outward corners on the diagonal, so a staircase becomes a straight cut. Rounded relaxes the contour so stairs become straight runs and corners round off. Render only: the collider stays on the cells. EdgeProfile.AmplitudeU/V, QuantiseU/V, DepthNoise The rim's jitter in the wall's plane, its banding, and the roughness of the crater's floor. Amplitude above 0.40 is refused: two neighbouring vertices would swap places. Keep Quantise around half the amplitude; at twice the amplitude or more every vertex rounds to zero and the axis has no jitter at all. Apply Preset warns about both. bBrittle, BrittleBreakFraction, BrittleShardSizeCm A brittle cell is whole or gone, so a pane never shows a dish or a dent. BrittleBreakFraction is the share of a cell's thickness one hit must take to break it for certain; smaller hits break it with a proportional chance, so a blast's edge cracks unevenly and repeated hits always get through. Lower it for thin panes, raise it for laminated glass. The pane is divided into irregular shards about BrittleShardSizeCm across, and a hit breaks out whole shards connected to the impact. The roll is made on the server, so every machine sees the same holes.

docs.title: Two kinds of brick
docs.text:
SurfaceType has six values and no Custom. That is deliberate: the enum is a lookup key for "what is this physically", for effects and sounds. Everything that differs between a red brick and a grey one lives on the preset.

You want Do this Two brick walls that break differently Two presets, both SurfaceType = Brick ...that also resist differently Point their SurfaceMaterialData at two different data assets Glass that shatters vs glass that spiders Two presets, different FractureWeightMask

docs.title: Size and structure
docs.text: ThicknessCm, CellDensity How deep the wall is, and cells per metre. Bigger cells hold more depth, so a wall that opens with no dent first wants a lower density or more thickness. SubdivisionFactor A cell splits into factor × factor fine children on its first bite. Detail, and its cost on the wire, exist only where the wall was hit. Raise it when a MASKSCALE line asks for it, or when an edge on show looks too smooth. StructuralThreshold The remaining fraction below which a cell stops carrying load. Wood gives up its load path long before it opens; reinforced concrete carries down to a shell; glass sheds whole panes at the first serious crack. MaxDestructionPercent The share of the wall that shooting may remove: 0 for a level boundary, 0.3 for a load-bearing element. Per wall, not per material, which is why the row is uniform. It gates shooting only: a severed piece still falls, and a collapse counts against the cap.

docs.title: MaxOverhangCm and BuiltOverhangs
docs.text:
A cell is held only if it is within MaxOverhangCm sideways of a column that stands on, or hangs from, a support. Up and down are free on an upright wall, so an intact wall always stands; a cantilever longer than the limit loses its tip, and a beam held at both ends spans twice the limit. On a ceiling or floor neither axis is free.

  • Keep it above half the widest opening with no wall under it, or the lintel over it falls on the first hit anywhere on the wall.
  • 0 turns it off. The limit is rounded down to whole cells.

What was built stands: the limit counts from how far a wall reached when damage first came to it, so it drops only what damage leaves overhanging. A wall built past the limit logs an OVERHANG line once. BuiltOverhangs on the preset (Wall | Durability, advanced) picks a stricter rule:

value a span built past the limit Keep (default) stands; the limit judges only what damage leaves SettleSilently is gone when the level starts, with no debris or sound Collapse comes down when the level starts, with debris and falling pieces

docs.title: Shape of a hit
docs.text: MinSpallRadiusCells The crater of a hit that brings no radius of its own (RadiusCm = 0). A weapon that passes a radius keeps it on a wall that subdivides, so a small round can leave a small mark without a denser grid; at SubdivisionFactor 1 this is the floor under every hit. If an edge looks too smooth, lower it to 0.8–1.0 on brick and concrete for a more local bite, and raise FractureNoise to keep small holes from reading as squares. Do not take it to 0. ExitSpallDepthScale, ExitSpallRadiusScale The blowout of the far face, as a fraction of the wall's thickness and a multiple of the hit's radius. It starts once the deepest cell in a hit is eaten past ThroughCouplingThreshold of the thickness (0.8 by default, on the wall's GridData component). Brittle materials throw more off the back; metal petals instead. 0 switches it off for the material. ObliquityStretch, ObliquitySkew A glancing hit becomes a furrow instead of a dish. The stretch lengthens the crater along the shot's direction; the skew slides it forward. Keep the two equal: that pins the trailing edge where a square-on crater's would be and sends all the added length forward. Below it the crater grows backwards, above it the crater leaves the impact point. FractureNoise, FractureNoiseScaleCm Varies each cell's resistance by a fixed amount, so a small hole does not read as a square. Above about 0.6 the rim turns noisy and specks survive inside holes. Clamped at 0.9. FractureMaskContrast, bDeriveFractureMaskFromMaterial Strength of the break pattern, and whether it comes from the wall material's height map. See Setup → Where the wall breaks. SpikeSuppressionChance, MinSupportingNeighbours Clean slivers off a hole's rim. A cell with fewer standing neighbours than the minimum is pruned with this chance. The chance is 0.7 on purpose: a rim with every spike pruned reads as machined. Keep the minimum at 2: higher strips the rim of every hole. By default the chance follows the break pattern, so brick cleans up along its joints and keeps its teeth on the bricks. SpikeSuppressionMask paints it per wall; SpikeMaskStrength sets how far a mask moves it.

docs.title: Edges and rims
docs.text: HoleRimThicknessFraction The band of wall left standing at a hole's edge, as a fraction of the thickness: what makes a hole read as a break in a solid rather than a cut in paper. Thin materials need more to show anything. It is also depth the crater cannot reach, so too much flattens craters; above about 0.5 a hole reads as a bevelled port. EdgeCrumbleScale How much an exposed edge (a capped side, a reveal) wanders as it erodes: crisp when intact, the material's own jitter when eaten. It needs a real EdgeProfile amplitude to show. RevealCrushScale A shot into a side (a reveal, a capped end, the bore of a hole) cuts that side along its own normal by PeakDepthCm × RevealCrushScale. 0 makes such a shot an ordinary face hit. CornerChipScale A shot at the face near an edge also chips the edge. Values near 1 make an edge give way about as fast as a shot straight into it; the shipped 4 makes corners crumble visibly faster than the face. Lower it toward 1–1.5 for a sturdier look. 0 switches it off. EdgeFirst In a cell at an edge, a face hit dents the face by 1 − EdgeFirst of its bite. At 1 the corner crumbles away before the face behind it gives. Does nothing while CornerChipScale is 0. DentStepCm Dents are drawn in whole steps of this depth, so a hit drops a chip instead of crumpling the face. A hit shallower than one step leaves the geometry flat and is shown by the damage material. The collider uses the same steps. 0 draws the exact depth. BreachFalloffCells Purely visual: how far, in cells, the "near a hole" channel of the damage material reaches. Glass at 4.0 is the deliberate outlier: its cracks radiate far past what was removed.

docs.title: CapEdges: closing the wall's own sides
docs.text:
Per placement, not per material. A wall's outer perimeter is open by default, because most walls are seated in a frame or a facade. Tick the sides a player can see:

the wall is tick seated in a frame, or flush between two others nothing protruding from another wall at 90° the exposed end only a free-standing barricade or a pillar of wall all four a panel whose top the player can see over Top

A cap breaks with the wall: it is built from the same cells as a hole's rim. If a capped edge looks like a knife edge, raise HoleRimThicknessFraction.

docs.title: Table 3: rubble
docs.text:
On the wall's GridCollapseVisual component, not on the preset.

Shipped values: open the table Concrete Brick Stone Wood Metal Glass DebrisMassScale 1.0 0.9 1.3 0.35 0.8 0.5 ChunkLifetimeSeconds 1.6 1.6 2.0 1.4 1.4 1.0 KeepSettledAboveSizeCm 0 0 0 0 0 0
  • Mass comes from the physical material first. Set PhysicalSurface on the preset; DebrisMassScale is taste on top. Leave it at 1.0 until the physical materials are in place.
  • Keep KeepSettledAboveSizeCm at 0 in multiplayer (it is read as 0 in any networked game). Rubble never replicates, so a piece left standing would be cover in a different place on every client that nothing can remove.

docs.title: Checking that a wall runs what the preset says
docs.text:
GridDestruction.CheckPresets

GRIDSTAMP [BP_Wall_Brick_7]: MATCH against preset 'GP_Brick' — ...
GRIDSTAMP [BP_Wall_Brick_9]: STALE against preset 'GP_Brick' — 1 field(s) differ:
    MinSupportingNeighbours live=2 preset=3. ...
GRIDSTAMP SUMMARY: 11 wall(s) — 1 stale, 0 without a preset, 10 current.

STALE means your edit never reached that wall: press Apply Preset on it and save the level. MATCH means the wall really runs the asset's values, so a knob that still looks inert is not a stamping problem. The same check runs on its own at BeginPlay on the server, and Log Preset Stamp Drift beside Apply Preset checks one wall. It reports and never corrects: a value set on the component alone is a legitimate per-wall override.

A Blueprint's own Class Defaults override the C++ defaults. If a knob does nothing, look at the placed actor's Details panel before anywhere else.

docs.title: Tuning order
docs.text: The tables are meant to be right on the first build. When a wall does not look like its material, work in this order, because each step changes what the next one is looking at. Change one number at a time.

docs.title: 1. Silhouette: does the hole have the right shape?
docs.text:
Look at one hole from the front.

what you see do the hole is a square raise FractureNoise, or give it a break pattern the rim is noisy rather than rough lower FractureNoise below 0.6 specks of wall survive inside the hole lower FractureNoise, or raise SpikeSuppressionChance the rim has no teeth raise EdgeProfile.AmplitudeU/V, or lower SpikeSuppressionChance brick cracks through the bricks, not the joints give it the material's height map, or raise FractureMaskContrast

docs.title: 2. Thickness: does the hole read as a break in a solid?
docs.text:
Look at the same hole from an angle.

what you see do the edge is a knife edge raise HoleRimThicknessFraction a visible band, but the crater looks shallow lower it the wall's own outer edge is open tick the right CapEdges a shot at a doorway's reveal dents the face raise RevealCrushScale a shot at the face next to an edge never chips it raise CornerChipScale the rim looks like the face, not like broken material use the damage material

docs.title: 3. Depth: does a hit dent before it opens?
docs.text:
Shoot the same spot repeatedly.

what you see do the wall opens with no dent first lower CellDensity, or raise ThicknessCm the crater is a flat disc raise EdgeProfile.DepthNoise the crater bottoms out early lower HoleRimThicknessFraction the far face stays flat until it opens lower ThroughCouplingThreshold on the wall, or raise ExitSpallDepthScale holes are crisp but cost too much lower SubdivisionFactor; see Multiplayer

docs.title: 4. Identity: is it the right material?
docs.text:
The three knobs that carry most of a material's identity, in order: FalloffScaleU/V, SmoothingAngleDeg, EdgeProfile.QuantiseU. DamageResistance comes last: it changes how many shots a wall takes, not how it looks.

Then fire along the wall:

what you see do a glancing hit leaves the same disc as a square one ObliquityStretch is 0: type table 2's row the furrow reaches behind where the round touched raise ObliquitySkew to equal ObliquityStretch the crater has left the impact point lower ObliquitySkew below ObliquityStretch a glancing hit on steel digs as deep as a square one RicochetAngleDeg is 0: type table 1's row

docs.title: 5. Weight: does the rubble belong to the wall?
docs.text: Author PhysicalSurface physical materials before touching DebrisMassScale.

docs.title: 6. The overlay: does the damage read as damage?
docs.text: See Damage material.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Most problems in a destruction setup are silent: they look like "nothing happened". The plugin logs a reason for almost every refusal, so start with the Output Log and the console commands below.

docs.title: Console commands
docs.text:
These need a running PIE session or game: the geometry and the grid exist only after BeginPlay.

command what it does GridDestruction.HashCells hashes every wall on every live world and prints a MATCH / MISMATCH verdict, naming the first differing cell GridDestruction.CheckPresets one line per wall: MATCH or STALE against its preset, plus walls over the late-join size GridDestruction.ShowSeams draws which walls are joined (green edges, yellow links) and logs each GRIDSEAM GridDestruction.RebuildWalls rebuilds every wall's visible mesh now GridDestruction.DumpGeometry audits winding, normals, counts and bounds on every wall GridDestruction.ProfileWall per-wall mesh statistics, including degen= (should be 0) and dropped= GridDestruction.ResetWalls every wall back to the damage it started with; on the server or standalone. docs.title: Slivers on a hole's rim
docs.text:
Why they appear. Every cell resists a little differently, by design: that is what stops small holes reading as squares. At the rim of a blast the bite is close to what a cell has left, so neighbouring cells flip independently and a few tough ones are left standing in the opening.

What removes them: MinSupportingNeighbours and SpikeSuppressionChance on the preset, shipping at 2 and 0.7. Two standing neighbours remove single spikes and pieces hanging by one edge, and keep anything with a shoulder on two sides. The chance is 0.7 rather than 1.0 on purpose: a rim with every spike pruned reads as machined.

  • By default the chance follows the break pattern, so brick cleans up along its joints and keeps its teeth on the bricks. SpikeMaskStrength turns that down.
  • Do not raise MinSupportingNeighbours above 2 to chase floating pieces: at 3 or 4 it strips the rim of every hole. Pieces nothing holds fall on their own; IslandCollapse in the log counts them.
  • Lowering FractureNoise and FractureMaskContrast makes rim cells behave more alike, at the cost of some raggedness.

The pass costs nothing on the network, and every machine prunes the same pieces. The log says how many pieces it pruned on every hit that removes something:

SpikeSuppression [Wall_0]: pruned 3 piece(s) ... minNeighbours=2 chance=0.70 mask=fracture weights strength=1.00

The wall's own border and the cells beside an authored opening are never pruned.

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text:
Write to annybelogurova@gmail.com with:

  • whether you saw it in the server window, the client window or both;
  • the output of GridDestruction.HashCells typed once while it is happening;
  • the log lines the plugin printed around it (they start with the wall's name in square brackets);
  • the engine version and whether the project is Blueprint-only.
